Issued at 318 AM EST Wed Nov 25 2026

Today through Friday Night...

A weak, mid-level disturbance is lifting northward this morning 
producing sprinkles to very light rain showers across central KY. 
The activity looks a lot more impressive on local WSR-88d KLVX, but 
with dewpoint values in the mid/upper 20s to low 30s, most of the 
activity is evaporating before it reaches the sfc. Where it has rain 
so far this morning across south central KY rainfall amounts have 
ranged from a trace to 0.003" of an inch. 

This weak wave is expected to lift northward into southern IN by 12z 
with any lingering shower activity becoming more isolated or 
dissipate. Once this passes, our CWA looks to remain mainly dry, cool 
and a little breezy for today. Highs are expected in the upper 40s 
to low 50s and we could see a few winds gusts of 20-25 mph. 

The main weather story remains the two upper lows and the impacts 
they will have across the central US, Ohio Valley and up and down 
the east coast of the CONUS. The strongest of the two is the upper 
low currently dropping south out of the Upper Midwest and expected 
to be in the Lower Mississippi Valley by Thanksgiving morning. 
While the weaker system coming out of of TX will move eastward along 
the Gulf Coast during the day, then help to develop and strengthen a 
sfc low off the GA/SC coast later tonight into tomorrow morning. As 
cyclogenesis increases with this system overnight, a strengthening 
LLJ over the Carolinas and VA will advect westward Atlantic moisture 
into into the TN and OH Valleys. The energy associated with the LLJ 
along with a westward moving inverted sfc trough will increase 
widespread rain showers over KY and the Ohio Valley later this 
evening and continue into Thanksgiving Day. PWAT values are expected 
to increase to around 1" late tonight into early Thursday morning 
leading to a period of widespread moderate rain showers. Total 
rainfall through Friday morning continues to range between 1 to 2" 
with the probability of exceeding 2 inches between 40-50 percent. 

Thursday into Thursday night our attention will turn to the strong 
upper level low over the the Lower Mississippi Valley as it is 
expected to move from MO/AR across KY/TN during the day and be over 
OH/PA/WV by Friday morning. This is the system that is expected to 
bring an impactful winter storm to parts of western IL and eastern 
MO later today into tonight. Once this system starts to move to the 
east-northeast Thursday, the colder air on the western side of this 
system will wrap around to the south and start to advect in over 
parts of KY and TN. Over the last 24 hours, model guidance has 
trended the core of the coldest air associated with this system 
further south into TN to right along the KY/TN border. By doing this 
it has also moved the chance of possible snow or rain/snow mix 
further south as well. We will continue to mention a chance of a 
rain/snow mix Thursday night into Friday morning but it is now for 
south of the parkways into TN. Temperatures tonight into 
Thanksgiving will not change much as we range from the low 40s by 
Thursday morning with daytime highs in the mid 40s. As the colder 
air associated with the upper-low Thursday night moves in 
temperatures will mainly stay above freezing with lows just near to 
slightly above 32 degrees. If there is any snow, only minor 
accumulations of a coating on elevated surface would be expected.  

The upper low and associated sfc low will lift off to the northeast 
and be in New England by Friday night. This will place us under 
northwest flow as moisture continues to wrap around the departing 
upper low. Friday will have a few scattered showers around during 
the day especially across southern IN into the Bluegrass. It will 
remain chilly with highs in the low/,mid 40s and blustery with gusty 
winds of 30-35 mph resulting in it feeling like it is in the low/mid 
30s. 


Saturday through Wednesday...

The upper level flow will flatten out and become more zonal for the 
day Saturday. We expect to be dry and even warmer with highs 
climbing into the mid/upper 50s thanks to a southerly flow. 

The next system to bring rain chances and possible thunderstorms 
will be associated with a shortwave trough coming out of the central 
Plains into the area on Sunday. We will still want to keep an eye on 
the potential for thunderstorms with this system as the trough still 
looks fairly strong with ECMWF but weaker on the GFS. As it was 
pointed out in the previous discussion, while instability remains 
lacking in model soundings, we still see steepening lapse rates 
Sunday afternoon and evening. 

The rest of the forecast looks to remain mainly dry and seasonable 
for late November as sfc high pressure builds in over the region for 
the start of the week.
